newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African budget relaxes exchange controls.
newsitem.headline: S.African budget relaxes exchange controls.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel took a significant step on Wednesday towards dismantling foreign exchange controls in a disciplined budget including severe expenditure cuts.
He left value added tax unchanged at 14 percent, cut personal tax by 2.8 billion rand and granted limited relief to companies and investors.

Delivering on a long-standing promise to narrow the gap between state income and expenditure, he estimated the budget deficit in the year to March 31, 1998, at 24.7 billion rand or four percent of gross domestic product, down from 5.1 percent.
Manuel's maiden budget was dominated by the announcement of measures to relax remaining exchange controls on South African nationals and residents.

"It is from our perspective a philosophical shift from a situation that has been essentially controlled, with a few exceptions, to one that is essentially free, with a few exceptions," he told a pre-budget news conference.
Manuel said in his budget speech individuals would be able to invest a limited amount directly abroad or alternatively hold foreign currency deposits with South African banks.
South African nationals and residents would for the first time be free to keep funds earned abroad outside the country.
The move will take effect from July 1 and specific ceilings will be announced before then, Manuel said.
Companies will also be given increased freedom to invest overseas and will be able to raise foreign funding on the strength of their South Africa balance sheet.

"We move now to an environment in which South Africans can make ordinary transactions abroad freely, while the constraints which remain on large movements of capital will increasingly give way to procedural and prudential supervision," he said.
Manuel announced expenditure plans totalling 186.7 billion rand, up 6.1 percent on last year, but substantially lower than the projected 8.5 percent inflation.
He estimated revenue, boosted by 2.5 billion from more efficient tax collection, but reduced by a 2.8 billion rand tax relief package, at 161.9 billion.
"This budget is a tough budget. It demands substantially more austerity from government than many of its forerunners have," Manuel told parliament in his budget address.
He added, however, that the government had not sacrificed its plan to transform South Africa's once white-ruled society and said poverty relief was a key focus of spending.

He allocated 40 billion rand to education, 20 billion to health care, 18 billion to welfare and four billion to housing. In a renewed assault on escalating crime, almost 30 billion rand was budgeted for police, defence, justice and prisons.
However, defence expenditure was down 667 million rand to 9.579 billion, the biggest loser.
"In this budget we make a substantial allocation to poverty relief. We invest in people through a significant reprioritisation of expenditures in favour of social development," Manuel said.
A budget review published as Manuel started to speak detailed tax proposals designed to ease the burden on people earning below 60,000 rand a year.
